title: Nine AI Messages for Students
author: Eric Hudson
summary: Hudson delivers nine messages to students about AI use in school after two years leading schools through adoption. The first two are paired. Using AI does not make a student good or bad; the moralized framing has hardened into unhelpful absolutism. But good uses and bad uses exist, and the line is the direct versus collaborative distinction. Direct use (tool produces the product) risks overreliance and degrades thinking. Collaborative use (tool supports you while you produce work) can deepen learning. The diagnostic: am I investing in a process or just generating a product. The middle messages map cheap signals (fluent prose as fluency, confident tone as authority, sycophantic warmth as care, conversational language as humanity) and argue AI is impersonal, not a companion. Four productive cases follow: fact-checking, upskilling, improving your own work through feedback, bringing ideas to life. The final three widen the lens. AI is a moment to practice your own ethics amid debates on bias and environmental cost. Current incentives push students toward hidden use; students should act from their best interest instead. Adults need students' help to bridge the 80/50 gap (80 percent of students use AI for schoolwork; 50 percent of teachers have never used it). The closing message matters most: keep the human in the loop by cultivating the kind of human who still wants to be in the loop.
points: The direct versus collaborative distinction is load-bearing: direct use (tool produces product) risks overreliance and degrades thinking, while collaborative use (tool supports while you produce) can deepen learning.
Cheap signals in AI output (fluent prose, confident tone, sycophantic warmth) are designed only to keep users engaged; they are not signals of truth, authority, or care.
Four productive uses of AI exist: fact-checking, upskilling, improving your own work through feedback, and bringing ideas to life; focus on these rather than on avoiding work.
Cultivating the kind of human who still wants to be in the loop, who feels the tug of curiosity and the satisfaction of earned insight, is what keeping the human in the loop actually means.
quotes: In my work I see a lot of uncritical celebration and shaming of people based on their AI use. Depending on your point of view, an AI enthusiast could be labeled innovative or immoral. An AI resistor could be labeled principled or out of touch. Using AI can be the right choice. Not using AI can also be the right choice.

Direct use is using AI to arrive at a solution as quickly as possible by asking it to complete a task for you. Collaborative use is using AI to assist you as you create work yourself. Anthropic found that about 50 percent of uses by college students were direct, and about 50 percent were collaborative.

If you are considering using AI for school, the most important question to ask yourself is, Am I investing in a process or am I just looking to generate a product? The former can deepen learning. The latter will not.

Chatbots have been designed to generate output quickly (a signal of fluency), deliver content with confidence (a signal of authority), take a responsive and sycophantic approach (a signal of care), and interact with us in natural, conversational language (a signal of humanity). These signals are cheap because they only make the chatbot appear fluent, authoritative, caring, and human so that we stay engaged with them.

AI is powerful, but it is not human. A LLM contains more information than your brain does, but it does not find that information meaningful. It can analyze patterns, make connections, and generate ideas faster than your brain might be able to, but it does not care about that work.

General purpose chatbots like ChatGPT would rather comfort you than warn you. They would rather keep you talking to them than encourage you to talk to a person. Their default mode is to endorse your ideas, not to question them.
Economics professor Jonathan Boymal puts it perfectly: You will not be replaced by AI, but by someone who has mastered their field deeply enough to take AI further than you can.

Recent surveys have found that while more than 80 percent of students have used AI for schoolwork, more than 50 percent of teachers have never used AI at all. What are we missing by not communicating across this gap?

Keeping the human in the loop has never been about inserting a person into a process that involves AI. It is about cultivating the kind of human who wants to be in the loop, who still feels the tug of curiosity, the satisfaction of an earned insight, the dignity of figuring something out.” Archived from Learning on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
